paras.text: Michigan Legal System and Method, Audio Lecture

This is the first chapter of the Michigan insurance law track, and I want to be honest with you about what it is. It is not a statute and it is not a case. It is the map. Every other chapter in this track sits on top of it, and if the map is solid, everything after it gets easier. If it is not, you will spend the later chapters memorizing things that never quite connect.

So here is what the map has on it. Which court hears an insurance case. Which document beats which when two sources disagree. How to read a citation so you can go find the real text yourself instead of taking somebody's word for it. What the Department of Insurance and Financial Services really is, and what it is not. And the clocks and boundaries, statutes of limitations and unauthorized practice of law, that sit underneath every claim fight you will study later.

I am going to teach you eleven ideas, one at a time. After most of them I will ask you a question and then go quiet while you answer it out loud. Answer out loud. The answer you can say is the answer you own.
Idea one. Which trial court, decided by the dollar amount.
Michigan splits its trial level jurisdiction mostly two ways: by how much money is in controversy, and by who the defendant is. Start with the money.

The district court has exclusive jurisdiction over civil actions where the amount in controversy does not exceed twenty five thousand dollars. That comes straight from M C L six hundred point eight three zero one. So a small water loss dispute, a few thousand dollars of contents, a fight over a deductible, that often starts and ends in district court.

Cross the twenty five thousand dollar line and you are in circuit court, Michigan's court of general jurisdiction. M C L six hundred point six zero five says circuit courts have original jurisdiction to hear and determine all civil claims and remedies, except where exclusive jurisdiction is given by the constitution or a statute to some other court.
Hear what that exception is doing. Circuit court is the default. It gets everything unless something specifically takes it away. That is what general jurisdiction means.
So most first party property insurance lawsuits, a homeowner suing a carrier over a denied or underpaid fire, water, or wind claim above twenty five thousand dollars, get filed in circuit court.

And circuit court shows up inside the appraisal process itself, which is worth holding onto now because you will meet it again. If the two appraisers cannot agree on a neutral umpire within fifteen days, either side can ask a judge of the circuit court, in the county where the loss happened or where the property sits, to pick the umpire. That is written directly into the standard fire policy statute.
Two numbers so far, and they do different jobs. Twenty five thousand dollars is the district court ceiling. Fifteen days is the umpire clock. Do not let them blur together.
Question for you. A homeowner is fighting over eighteen thousand dollars of contents. Which trial court, and what is the number that decides it. Say it out loud.
District court, because eighteen thousand does not exceed twenty five thousand dollars, and the section is M C L six hundred point eight three zero one.
Idea two. The Court of Claims, and the trap inside it.

This is the court that trips people up, so let me name the trap before I explain the court. The word claims is doing something dishonest to your ear. You work in insurance claims. This court has nothing to do with insurance claims.

The Court of Claims is a statewide court, housed at the Court of Appeals, and it has exclusive jurisdiction over money, equitable, or declaratory claims against the State of Michigan or its departments and officers.
That is the whole key phrase: against the state.

So think about who you actually sue in this work. State Farm. Auto Owners. A third party administrator. Every one of those is a private company. Suing a private insurance company is not a claim against the state, so it belongs in circuit court. The Court of Claims only comes in if you are suing a state agency itself.
Question. You are suing an insurance carrier for two hundred thousand dollars on a denied fire claim. Does the word claim put you in the Court of Claims.
No. Circuit court. The Court of Claims is about who the defendant is, the State of Michigan, not about the word claim.
Idea three. The two courts above, and how you get to each one.

Above circuit court sits the Court of Appeals, the intermediate appellate court. The thing to know is the phrase jurisdiction as of right, which means no permission needed. The Court of Appeals has jurisdiction as of right over final judgments and final orders from the circuit court, the Court of Claims, and the probate court.

Some other orders are not as of right. An appeal from a guilty plea, or certain interlocutory orders, meaning orders in the middle of a case rather than at the end, are only reviewable if the Court of Appeals grants leave.

Here is why you should care about that court specifically. Nearly every published Michigan insurance case you will study in the chapters ahead, the ones setting the rules on policy interpretation, bad faith, and appraisal, came out of the Court of Appeals.

At the very top sits the Michigan Supreme Court, the court of last resort. It generally takes cases by leave, meaning it chooses which appeals to hear, and once it rules, that ruling binds every lower court in the state. Nickola versus M I C General, decided by the Supreme Court in May of twenty seventeen, is exactly that kind of case.
So the pair to hold is as of right versus by leave. Court of Appeals, as of right from a final judgment. Supreme Court, by leave, its choice.
Idea four. Let me walk one case up the ladder so it stops being abstract.
A homeowner's eighty thousand dollar fire claim gets denied.
Eighty thousand is above the twenty five thousand dollar district court ceiling, so it starts in circuit court.

The insurer wins summary disposition, which we will get to, and the homeowner appeals. That goes to the Court of Appeals as a matter of right, because what is being appealed is a circuit court final judgment.
And then it stops, unless the Supreme Court agrees to grant leave.
Notice what that example is really teaching. The dollar amount picked the starting court. The finality of the judgment made the first appeal automatic. And nothing after that is automatic at all.
Idea five. Published versus unpublished, and what unpublished actually means.

This is governed by Michigan Court Rule seven point two one five, subsection C. Here is the rule almost word for word. An unpublished opinion is not precedentially binding under the rule of stare decisis. Unpublished opinions should not be cited for propositions of law where published authority already exists, and a party who does cite one must explain why and how it is relevant.
Compare that to a published opinion, which has precedential effect under stare decisis, and that effect does not go away just because somebody asks the Supreme Court to review it.

Now the plain English, because this is where people go wrong in both directions. Unpublished does not mean useless, and it does not mean forbidden. It means not binding. A trial court can find an unpublished opinion persuasive and follow its reasoning, and it is equally free to reach a different conclusion.

Tredenick, a twenty twenty one Court of Appeals decision out of the adjuster licensing world, docket number three four nine eight eight seven, is exactly this kind of opinion. Unpublished. Persuasive only. Never treated as settled law. You will meet it again in the licensing chapter, and when you do, that is the label it carries.

One more piece. Publication is not automatic. The court rule lists eight standards, things like establishing a new rule of law, resolving a first impression question about a statute, or reversing existing law. If none of them apply, the opinion is deemed unpublished by default.
And when you want the actual text of any opinion, published or not, or the current Michigan Court Rules themselves, go to courts dot michigan dot gov.
Question. Somebody hands you an unpublished Court of Appeals opinion that says exactly what you want it to say. What is it worth in court.

It is persuasive, not binding. The judge may follow it or may not, and you should not lean on it where published authority already covers the point. If you do cite it, you have to explain why and how it is relevant.
Idea six. The instrument hierarchy, which is the single most useful idea in this chapter.
When two sources disagree, you need to know which one wins. In Michigan insurance work you will hit four types constantly, and they rank.
At the top, a statute. An M C L section, passed by the legislature and signed into law. That is primary, binding law. It changes only if the legislature amends or repeals it.

Below that, an administrative rule. One of the Michigan Administrative Code's R numbers, adopted by an agency like D I F S under delegated authority. It is binding, but it is subordinate to the statute that authorized it, and it can be struck down if the agency exceeded that authority.

Below that, a D I F S bulletin. Interpretive guidance, explaining how the department reads an existing statute or rule. It is not independent law. The department can reissue it or withdraw it at any time, with no legislative process at all. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S, the one limiting labor depreciation on actual cash value payments, is a bulletin. Not a statute. It has a very real practical effect on what carriers do, and it is still a bulletin.

And at the very bottom, a pending bill, which has zero legal force until it passes both chambers and is signed. Senate Bill two forty five, proposing a first party bad faith cause of action, is the live example. It was reported favorably out of committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole. It has not passed either chamber. It is not law. Treat it as pending until that changes, and be suspicious of anybody who talks about it as though it already happened.

Now a trap inside this idea, and it is a good one because the number looks so promising. Rule five hundred point two two zero two sounds like it should be a matching rule, the kind of thing you would want when a carrier will only pay for half a roof of siding. It is not. It is actually titled discretionary clauses prohibited. Michigan has no matching statute and no matching administrative rule at all.
Question. A carrier's adjuster tells you a D I F S bulletin requires them to do something, and the statute plainly says otherwise. Which one controls, and why.

The statute. A bulletin is interpretive guidance about how the department reads the law, it is not independent law, and the department can withdraw it tomorrow. Statute beats rule, rule beats bulletin, and a pending bill is worth nothing at all.
Idea seven. Reading a citation, so you can go look it up yourself.
Take M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision m.

Five hundred is the chapter number, and chapter five hundred is the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, formally Act two eighteen of nineteen fifty six. Two eight three three is the section. The one in parentheses is subsection one. The m is subdivision m. Read out loud, that is act two eighteen of nineteen fifty six, section twenty eight thirty three, subsection one, subdivision m.

The same logic works for chapter six hundred, which is the Revised Judicature Act of nineteen sixty one, Act two thirty six of nineteen sixty one. That is the one governing Michigan's courts, jurisdiction, and civil procedure, including statutes of limitations and unauthorized practice of law. So when you see a section starting with six hundred, you are in the courts and procedure book. Five hundred, you are in the insurance book. That one habit will orient you instantly.

Court rules follow a similar pattern. M C R two point one one six, subsection C, subsection ten. Chapter two is civil procedure. Subrule C lists the grounds for summary disposition. Sub subrule ten is the specific ground about no genuine issue of material fact.

Case citations work differently. Instead of a chapter and section you get a volume and a page in an official reporter. Four oh nine Mich four oh one means volume four hundred nine of the Michigan Reports, page four hundred one. And here is the tell worth memorizing: Mich with no App always signals a Supreme Court opinion. That one is Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance, decided in nineteen eighty.

Now the pair. Two seventy six Mich App five fifty one. Mich App means the Michigan Appeals Reports, which is Court of Appeals opinions. That one is Griswold Properties versus Lexington Insurance, decided in two thousand seven.
Mich, Supreme Court. Mich App, Court of Appeals. That is the whole trick, and it is two letters.

And an unpublished opinion never gets a reporter volume or page at all, which is why you cite it by docket number and decision date instead. That is why Tredenick came to you as docket three four nine eight eight seven rather than a volume and page.
Question. You see two seventy six Mich App five fifty one, and you see four oh nine Mich four oh one. Which court decided each one, and how do you know.
Two seventy six Mich App five fifty one is the Court of Appeals, because of the App. Four oh nine Mich four oh one is the Supreme Court, because Mich with no App means Supreme Court.
Idea eight. What D I F S can do, and what it cannot.
People badly misunderstand this one, and the misunderstanding costs homeowners real time.

Start with what the department says about itself. D I F S provides consumer information, investigates consumer complaints, and works to assist consumers in resolving those complaints whenever possible. Listen to that phrasing. Assist in resolving whenever possible. And the department encourages you to try resolving a dispute with the company directly first.

Now the teeth, because it does have some. When you file a complaint, D I F S investigates. If it finds that a licensed adjuster, solicitor, or insurance counselor violated the Insurance Code's licensing chapter, the director can order real consequences after a hearing. A cease and desist order. A civil fine. A refund of overcharges. Restitution to the insured for losses caused by that violation. And suspension or revocation of the license.
That is a serious list. Now here is the boundary, and this is the part to hold.

D I F S cannot act as your personal attorney. It cannot make a binding factual determination about who is right in a disputed coverage question. And it does not order a private insurer to simply pay a claim the way a court judgment can.

Even the restitution power is narrower than it sounds. It only reaches a licensee who was found, after a D I F S hearing, to have violated the licensing chapter. That is not D I F S stepping in as a judge to award general breach of contract or bad faith damages in a routine coverage fight.

So here is the practical sorting rule. If what you want is money out of an insurer, the tool is a lawsuit in circuit court, or appraisal where it applies. D I F S is the right tool for a licensing violation or a pattern of unfair practices. It is the wrong tool if what you want is a payment ordered.
Question. Homeowner says the carrier underpaid her fire claim by forty thousand dollars and she wants D I F S to make them pay it. What do you tell her.

D I F S will investigate, and it may act against a licensee who violated the licensing chapter, but it will not decide the disputed coverage question for her and it will not order the carrier to pay the claim. For the money, the tool is circuit court, or appraisal if it applies.
Idea nine. The shape of a lawsuit, start to finish.
You do not need to litigate one. You need to recognize where a case is standing when somebody tells you about it.

It starts with a complaint, where the person suing states the facts, the legal claims, and what they want. The other side files an answer, admitting or denying each allegation and raising defenses, maybe a statute of limitations defense, maybe an exclusion argument.

Then discovery. Both sides exchange documents like the policy and the claim file. They send written interrogatories under rule two point three zero nine. They take depositions under rule two point three zero six, which is sworn out of court testimony.

After discovery, either side can move for summary disposition, asking the judge to decide some or all of the case without a trial. The most common ground in insurance fights is the one I gave you earlier, M C R two point one one six, subsection C, subsection ten. Except as to the amount of damages, there is no genuine issue as to any material fact, and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
In plain words: if the facts that matter are not really in dispute, and the law clearly points one way, the judge can end the case without a jury.

And if the case survives that, it goes to trial. But a jury is not automatic, and this is the detail people lose. Under Michigan Court Rule two point five zero eight, a party must file a written jury demand, as a separate document, within twenty eight days after the answer, and pay the jury fee. Miss that window and the issues are tried by the judge alone, which is a bench trial.
Hear all three parts of that requirement. Written. Separate document. Twenty eight days after the answer. Plus the fee.
Idea ten. The two clocks, and why the short one is not as short as it looks.

Michigan's default statute of limitations for an ordinary breach of contract claim is six years. That is M C L six hundred point five eight zero seven, subsection nine, the catch all for contract actions not described elsewhere in that section.

A fire insurance policy does not get that six year window, because the standard fire policy statute writes its own, much shorter clock directly into the policy. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision q, requires suit within one year after the loss, or the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer.
Stop on that phrase, whichever is longer. It makes one year a floor, not a ceiling. A policy cannot shorten it below one year. A longer contractual period would control.
Six years for ordinary contract. One year floor for the fire policy. That is the pair, and the exam of real life will hand you the wrong one.

Now the tolling rule built into that same subdivision, because it changes the math completely. The clock pauses entirely from the moment the insured notifies the insurer until the insurer formally denies liability. Tolled just means paused. Not running at all.
Let me do the arithmetic with you.
A pipe bursts in a basement on March first. The homeowner reports it that same day. The insurer investigates for four months and does not formally deny the claim until July first.

Her one year clock did not run during those four months. It was tolled from notice until formal denial. So her effective filing window runs close to a full year from July first, not from the March first date of loss.
If you had counted from the date of loss, you would have told her she was nearly four months worse off than she actually is. That is the practical value of knowing one sentence of one subdivision.
Question. Loss on January tenth, reported January tenth, formally denied on June tenth. Roughly when does her window close, and what is the rule that gets you there.

Roughly June tenth of the following year. The one year clock under M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision q, was tolled from notice until formal denial, so those five months did not count against her.
Idea eleven. Unauthorized practice of law, and two statutes that are not interchangeable.
Do not confuse these two, because they solve completely different problems, and the confusion is the kind that gets a contractor in trouble.

The first is the general rule, M C L six hundred point nine one six. It says a person shall not practice law, shall not lead others to believe they are authorized to practice law, and shall not call themselves an attorney, unless actually licensed to practice law in Michigan. The penalty is contempt of the supreme court and of the circuit court of the county where the violation happened, punishable as provided by law. The statute carves out one narrow exception: an attorney licensed in another state, temporarily in Michigan, handling one specific matter, does not violate it.

The second lives deep inside the insurance code. M C L five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a, exempts a person admitted to the practice of law in Michigan from needing a separate adjuster's license. That subsection lists exactly five exemptions. The attorney. A marine average adjuster. An insurer's own employee adjusting under the insurer's policy. A licensed producer with claim authority. And a supervised data entry clerk.

Now hear the difference, because it is the whole idea. Six hundred point nine one six stops a non lawyer from practicing law or pretending to be a lawyer. Five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a, only tells you that a lawyer who is already licensed does not also need a separate adjuster license.

And here is the trap that matters to you personally. A contractor cannot borrow that exemption by working alongside an attorney, or by being related to one. It belongs to the licensed attorney personally, and to no one else.
Question. A contractor says he can handle claims for homeowners without an adjuster license because his brother is a lawyer. Which statute is he misreading, and what is wrong with it.

He is misreading M C L five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a. That exemption belongs to the licensed attorney personally. It is not transferable, not to a relative and not to a coworker.
Time for the rapid fire recap. I am going to say these fast. You are not learning them now, you are checking which ones you already have.

District court, twenty five thousand dollars or less, M C L six hundred point eight three zero one. Circuit court above that, general jurisdiction, M C L six hundred point six zero five. Circuit court picks the umpire if the appraisers cannot agree in fifteen days. Court of Claims, only against the State of Michigan. Court of Appeals, as of right from final judgments of circuit, Court of Claims, and probate. Supreme Court, by leave, binds everyone, Nickola versus M I C General, May twenty seventeen. Michigan Court Rule seven point two one five, subsection C, unpublished is not binding, persuasive only, eight publication standards, unpublished by default if none apply. Tredenick, twenty twenty one, docket three four nine eight eight seven, unpublished. Hierarchy, statute, then administrative rule, then D I F S bulletin, then pending bill with no force. Rule five hundred point two two zero two is discretionary clauses prohibited, not matching, and Michigan has no matching rule. Bulletin twenty twenty four dash twenty six dash I N S, labor depreciation, is a bulletin. Senate Bill two forty five, pending, not law. Chapter five hundred is the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, Act two eighteen. Chapter six hundred is the Revised Judicature Act of nineteen sixty one, Act two thirty six. M C R two point one one six, subsection C, subsection ten, summary disposition, no genuine issue of material fact. Interrogatories two point three zero nine, depositions two point three zero six. Jury demand, M C R two point five zero eight, written, separate document, twenty eight days after the answer, plus the fee. Mich means Supreme Court, Mich App means Court of Appeals. Four oh nine Mich four oh one is Kewin, nineteen eighty. Two seventy six Mich App five fifty one is Griswold Properties versus Lexington, two thousand seven. D I F S can order cease and desist, civil fine, refund of overcharges, restitution, suspension or revocation, and cannot be your attorney, cannot decide a disputed coverage question, cannot order a claim paid. Contract statute of limitations, six years, M C L six hundred point five eight zero seven, subsection nine. Fire policy suit, one year floor, M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one, subdivision q, whichever is longer, tolled from notice to formal denial. Unauthorized practice of law, M C L six hundred point nine one six, contempt, one exception for an out of state attorney on one matter. Adjuster license exemption, M C L five hundred point one two two two, subsection two, subdivision a, five exemptions, attorney, marine average adjuster, insurer's employee, producer with claim authority, supervised data entry clerk.

That is the whole map. Courts by dollar amount and by defendant. Precedent that depends on publication. An instrument hierarchy running from statute down to a bill that is worth nothing. Citations that tell you exactly where to look. A regulator that investigates but is not your lawyer and cannot order payment. The stages of a lawsuit. And two very different clocks, six years and one year, with a tolling rule that quietly gives months back.
Carry this chapter into every one that follows. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is your signal for where to drill.
